verdict.reasoning: Patient reports being “wheezy” and “short of breath” for “two, three days” and says walking to work is no longer possible and that sometimes it is “quite difficult to complete the talking… sometimes,” indicating exertional worsening and occasional speech limitation.

Patient reports “I have cough and cough a lot” but denies phlegm and blood (“No” to phlegm, “No, I don’t think so” to blood). They say they “have a fever” but measured temperature was “thirty seven,” and doctor confirms that is normal. Patient denies chest pain (“No chest pain, no”) and nocturnal symptoms (“No, just daytime working, yeah”). This supports a dry cough, subjective fever with measured 37°C, no chest pain, no nocturnal symptoms, and no sputum or hemoptysis.

Patient had asthma in childhood and adulthood, last using regular medications “Few years ago, like, three or four years ago.” Currently they report using salbutamol: “Um, I took salbutamol… Normally, yeah” and “Every, every few weeks? I’m not sure,” and that they use inhalers with exercise (“What about when you exercise…? Patient: Yeah”). This supports a flare now with last regular asthma medication years ago, salbutamol use every few weeks, and exercise-induced symptoms.

Patient states, “Yes, I had asthma. I also had, uh, hay fever and eczema,” and that asthma was present as a child and also as an adult, consistent with childhood-to-adult asthma plus hay fever and eczema.
Patient confirms current use: “Um, I took salbutamol? … Normally, yeah,” and describes frequency “Every, every few weeks,” consistent with as-needed salbutamol inhaler use.
When asked about allergies, the patient replies, “No, no allergies,” indicating no known drug allergies.

Patient states, “I live with my partner,” occupation “I’m engineer,” smoking: “No, I don’t smoke,” and alcohol: “one glass of wine… Every two or three days? Depends, yeah,” supporting the social history described.

Doctor says, “it sounds like you’ve had a flare up of your asthma. It could be, um, triggered by… more pollen around, or… a viral infection.” Patient denies rest dyspnea (“at the moment… feeling short of breath when you’re sitting still? … Patient: No”) and has a temperature of “thirty seven,” which the doctor calls “fine,” supporting a mild asthma exacerbation with suggested triggers and no rest dyspnea or objective fever.
Patient explicitly reports, “I also had, uh, hay fever,” and later, “I have, uh, hay fever as well,” which is consistent with allergic rhinitis/hay fever.
Doctor advises, “if you increase it so you’re taking it two to four puffs, like, every four hours? Initially,” which matches salbutamol 2–4 puffs every 4 hours as needed for the current flare.

Doctor says, “I can prescribe you… a spacer to use your inhaler a bit more efficiently, which the pharmacist can show you how you use that when you pick it up,” confirming spacer prescription and pharmacist teaching.

Doctor states, “I can prescribe you a peak flow meter… and then if you… record a value first thing when you wake up… And in the evening over the next week,” which matches prescribing a peak-flow meter with AM/PM readings for 1 week.

Doctor instructs, “if you get a high temperature or your wheezing is getting worse, you need to call us back straightaway so we can just advise you further,” providing explicit safety-netting for deterioration.

Doctor proposes, “it will be a good idea when you’re feeling better if we can arrange just a review… You could arrange a review in a week or so,” and notes “we may need to start some other medication for you,” consistent with a follow-up tele-review in ~1 week with possible controller inhaler consideration.

Doctor advises, “the other thing to do would be to take a regular antihistamine. Which you can get from the pharmacy,” which corresponds to starting a daily over-the-counter antihistamine for hay fever.
